accuracy.evidence: Weather words and clothing choices checked against Development Matters 2021 (3 and 4 year olds talk about differences and changes they notice; Reception: effect of changing seasons), the Year 1 programme of study (observe and describe weather associated with the seasons), Met Office explanations that fog is cloud at ground level and wind is moving air, and NHS sun-safety advice (hat, sun cream, shade around midday). Snow on a sunny day is treated as cold, which is correct.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors young children make: sun always means warm (sunny-but-snowy step and challenge), every grey sky is rainy (look step feedback and m6), wind is visible (wind prediction), an umbrella helps in strong wind (challenge 'umb' and m7), and a cosy woolly jumper is fine in rain (rain prediction and the soaked-jumper message).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwear is a dressing lab: a child figure in a weather scene, ten drawn garments in body, feet and head slots that replace each other, and a Go outside test that judges the outfit per weather. No other flag lab dresses a figure or animates rain, snow and wind; the 6-token shingle gate passed against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers by testing: going outside in a jumper says the rain soaks in, sandals give wet toes, a coat in hot sun says too hot, and a sun hat on a snowy day says snow is cold. Only the outfit that does the job gets 'Just right' and a hop, so the reason comes from the test, not from being told.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions: woolly jumper vs raincoat for rain (cosy is tempting, the soak message disproves it), whether you can see the wind (a grey cloud is offered, the wind step shows only moving things), and sun hat vs woolly hat when the sun shines on snow (the sun hat fails the outdoor test).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions, each wrong option tagged: cloud and fog explain falling drops mean rain, umb and warm say an umbrella does not stop wind and can blow inside out, sunsnow and thin say snow is cold, toes and socks say water gets in, hot and hot2 say coats and woolly hats overheat, blue and cold say look for moving things.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid text scores FK 0.3 with four short paragraphs of one idea each, adult text FK 9.7 under the 10.0 limit. Exact terms for the age band: weather, observe, season, waterproof, sunny, rainy, cloudy, foggy, windy, snowy; fog defined as cloud at ground level and wind as moving air.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean and explanation overlap under 12 percent. Every kid sentence names a weather or a garment and its job; adult paragraphs give the curriculum statements, the clues to look for, named mistakes and what each lab step does, with no stock openings.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in both themes for the window, rain, wind, snow and challenge steps: garment cards sit in two rows of five with labels readable at 11 px bold, the weather buttons wrap in rows of three, and the outfit result pill sits under the child without clipping. walk.cjs passes on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark. Every garment has a toggle button with aria-pressed besides drag and tap, Go outside is a button, wind targets have buttons, and the canvas aria-label and live description repeat every result. Rain and snow motion stop under reduced motion.

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: Understanding the World, The Natural World (3 and 4 year olds; Reception)
DfE (2013) National curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 1 Seasonal changes
Met Office: What is fog? and What is wind? (learn about weather pages)
